200.description:
One film's identity and rating from its Letterboxd page: slug, lid (boxd.it short id), numeric film id, name, year, earliest release date with its release type (a festival premiere for most festival films; the theatrical dates are in releases), canonical and short URLs, TMDB and IMDb ids, runtime, description, tagline, poster, directors, cast, the full crew by role (writer, producer, editor, cinematography, composer and so on), genres, countries, languages, studios, alternative titles, release dates by type and country with certification, the Similar Films strip, and the weighted average rating with rating and review counts (null when Letterboxd shows no rating yet). The response contains the tool result directly.

value.description:
IMDB's top 250 list: loved by some, hated by others. Of course you can argue about the order of movies and the presence or absence of certain titles. Fact remains that it holds a great deal of the most appreciated films of all time and the overall quality is pretty high.

I tried to complete the list once, but choked near the end... ;-) I will keep updating weekly though and one day I will finish the last few missing films.

Feel free to comment your % or must sees from this list!
And for the people who find 250 entries a bit lacking, here's a list with every movie that was once in IMDB's Top 250.

A few statistics...

The oldest movie on the list is Charlie Chaplin's The Kid, released in 1921. The most popular decade in the list is the 2000's with 49 entries. A complete overview:
1920's - 6 entries
1930's - 6 entries
1940's - 9 entries
1950's - 21 entries
1960's - 16 entries
1970's - 19 entries
1980's - 25 entries
1990's - 39 entries
2000's - 49 entries
2010's - 41 entries
2020's - 19 entries

Christopher Nolan is the king of IMDB, with 9 films on the top 250. There are three directors with 7 films on the list. Scorsese, Kubrick and Spielberg complete the crème de la crème according to IMDB users.

All popular directors:
9 entries - Christopher Nolan
7 entries - Stanley Kubrick, Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese
6 entries - Akira Kurosawa, Quentin Tarantino
5 entries - Billy Wilder, Charlie Chaplin, Alfred Hitchcock
4 entries - Hayao Miyazaki, Sergio Leone
3 entries - Brad Bird, Clint Eastwood, David Fincher, Francis Ford Coppola, James Cameron, Joel Coen, Pete Docter, Peter Jackson, Ridley Scott, Denis Villeneuve


Latest update: 28/9/2026. I am currently at 98%

Back in the list:
Miracle in Cell No. 7 at #250

Gone, not forgotten:
Andhadhun

reviews.text:
Update: Now in video form

There is a house on a hill, and there are people in it. And they're nice, but not really. There is a garden, and there they get a lot of sunlight. And it is nice, and they get to sleep there sometimes.

There is a house underground, and there are people in it. And they're the first to tell you that they're not very nice: they're con-men, grifters, forgers and imposters. They sit among stink bugs, and they've been there for so long that maybe they've convinced themselves that they just belong there.

There is a rock, and it is a gift, but it is also a burden. And maybe it's a metaphor, but it's also just a rock: solid and heavy, difficult to lug around, and dangerous in the wrong hands. Some people will tell you that it's supposed to bring wealth. But again, it's also just a rock.

There is a line, and it cannot be crossed.

There is a smell, and it comes from the underground. And the people who live in the house on the hill can smell it. And the people who live underground try to imagine a life in the sun, a future where they aren't just garbage to be washed away in the rain. But there is a smell that sticks to them, and they know that they can never really belong.

There is a world, and it is nice, but not really. There are houses on hills, and houses underground. There is plenty of sun, but it isn't for everybody. There are people grateful to be slaves, and people unhappy to be served. There are systems that we are born into, and they create these lines that cannot be crossed. And we all dream of something better, but we've been living with these lines for so long that we've convinced ourselves that there really isn't anything to be done.

There is a knife. And it doesn't do much in the long run, but there will always be some satisfaction in crossing some lines.

One film's member reviews, twelve per page, from the public /film/{slug}/reviews/ pages: review id and boxd.it short id, review URL, full text (a preview the page truncates is expanded through the /s/full-text/ fragment), star rating (null when the member gave none), liked and rewatch flags, watched date, reviewer handle and display name, like count, comment count, spoiler flag and language. Sort `popular` is the film page's Popular reviews order; `newest`, `earliest`, `highest_rated` and `lowest_rated` are the page's other sorts. `next_page` continues.

The response contains the tool result directly.

The provider identifies `reviews` as the primary payload key.

| Documented field | Provider type | Description |

| `rating` | number | Stars on the 0.5-5 scale; null when the review carries no rating. |

| `url` | string | Review page URL (/<member>/film/<slug>/). |
